newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine opposition unions march for jobs.
newsitem.headline: Argentine opposition unions march for jobs.

text.p: Argentine opposition trade unions marched on Buenos Aires' landmark Plaza de Mayo on Friday in a fresh protest against high unemployment and the Peronist government's plans for labour law reforms.

President Carlos Menem's message to the marchers led by the MTA and CTA labour federations, with the support of the Radical Party and Frepaso coalition, was curt: "They can stage a thousand marches but nothing will change," he told reporters.
The core opposition to Menem, and to the main CGT union federation which has signed a labour law reform deal with him, planned to stage an afternoon rally outside government house.
Hardline state workers' leader Carlos "Mad Dog" Santillan, from the poor northwest, headed a column of 50 buses.

"Putting an end to Menemism is the only way we can move forward," he told supporters, denouncing the CGT as "traitors" and saying Menem has brought Argentina "more hunger, more unemployment and more desperation."

The jobless rate has more than doubled since Menem came to power in 1989 to 17.3 percent, making it the top issue for mid-term elections in Congress in October. But Menem has dismissed roadblock protests up and down the country as "subversion", and argues that robust economic growth combined with more modern labour laws will create jobs.
Officials predict the next release of twice-yearly job data on July 18 will show the jobless rate has fallen to 16 percent.

Menem instructed his cabinet to publicise the billions of dollars of public works projects being announced before the elections. While acknowledging "some sort of discontent in the heart of our community," he promised investors there would be no change in the economic policy that has reduced inflation to zero from 4,000 in 1989.

"For your peace of mind, there is no possibility of change in the direction this government has chosen in politics, economics and in social and international programmes," he said in a speech at the stock exchange on Thursday.

But the unionists on the march do not buy Menem's promises on jobs. The MTA and CTA both shun the much-larger CGT, which is traditionally close to the government, for signing a pact on labour reforms awaiting congressional approval. The deal is also opposed by big business, which wants labour "flexibilization" to scrap union control of pay talks and redundancy payouts.
"The real worry is unemployment: 2.6 million comrades out of work are the real unwritten law of flexibilization," Victor de Gennaro of the CTA told reporters.
Truckdrivers' leader Hugo Moyano of the MTA scoffed at "pharaonic" public works projects and asked where were the 300,000 jobs Menem promised when re-elected in May 1995.
"The truth is Argentina is more and more desperate. Today we will see the real Argentina the government wants to hide, the Argentina of unemployment and poor pay," said Moyano.
